facts: Manchester Cathedral has the widest nave of any cathedral in England.
It suffered severe bomb damage in the 1940 Manchester Blitz and again in the 1996 IRA bombing nearby.
Manchester Victoria station sits right beside the cathedral in the city centre.
The museum is built partly on the site of the world's first passenger railway station, Liverpool Road, opened 1830.
It houses a working replica of the pioneering locomotive Planet.
Manchester was the site of the Industrial Revolution's cotton-spinning boom, earning the nickname 'Cottonopolis'.
The library was built in memory of textile magnate John Rylands by his widow, opening in 1900.
Its neo-Gothic reading room is one of the most striking library interiors in Britain.
Manchester Piccadilly is the city's principal railway station.
Old Trafford has been Manchester United's home ground since 1910 and is the largest club football stadium in England.
The station is only open on match days and major event days.
It sits close to Old Trafford cricket ground, Lancashire's home venue, a short distance away.
MediaCityUK is home to major BBC and ITV production studios, opened from 2011.
Salford Quays was once the busiest part of the Manchester Ship Canal's dock system.
The Lowry arts centre and Imperial War Museum North both sit within the redeveloped quays.
Manchester Airport is the busiest airport in the UK outside London.
The station sits directly beneath the terminal buildings.
It is a key interchange for services from across the North West.
Carnforth station's clock and platform famously featured in the 1945 film Brief Encounter.
The station's refreshment room has been restored to its wartime film appearance.
Carnforth was once a major railway junction on the West Coast Main Line.
Windermere is England's largest natural lake, over 17 kilometres long.
The station is the only railhead directly serving the central Lake District.
The nearby town of Bowness-on-Windermere is a major hub for lake cruises.
Buxton was developed as a Georgian and Victorian spa town, exploiting its natural thermal springs.
The Buxton Crescent, modelled on Bath's Royal Crescent, has been restored as a five-star hotel and spa.
At over 300 metres above sea level, Buxton is one of the highest market towns in England.
Tatton Park is one of the most complete historic estates in England, with a mansion, farm and deer park.
It hosts the RHS Tatton Park Flower Show each year.
Knutsford's Georgian streets inspired Elizabeth Gaskell's novel Cranford.
Blackpool Tower, opened in 1894, was inspired by the Eiffel Tower and stands 158 metres tall.
Blackpool's Illuminations have lit the seafront every autumn since 1879.
Blackpool North is the town's principal railway station.
The Harris Museum is a grand neoclassical building in the heart of Preston.
Preston was a centre of the cotton industry and a site of early trade union organisation.
The Guild Merchant, a civic celebration held roughly every 20 years, dates back to 1179.
Wigan Pier was made famous by George Orwell's 1937 book The Road to Wigan Pier, documenting industrial poverty.
The 'pier' was actually a coal loading staithe on the Leeds and Liverpool Canal, not a seaside pier.
Wigan Wallgate serves the town's canal-side heritage quarter.
The Rochdale Pioneers founded the modern cooperative movement here in 1844.
Their original shop on Toad Lane is preserved as a museum.
Rochdale was a major centre of the Lancashire cotton and woollen industries.
Todmorden sits right on the historic border between Yorkshire and Lancashire.
Its grand Town Hall, built in 1875, straddles the county boundary.
The town became known for its 'Incredible Edible' community food-growing movement.
Glossop is a gateway town to the Dark Peak, part of the Peak District National Park.
The town was largely built by the Wood family as a model industrial community in the 19th century.
Nearby Old Glossop retains a much older medieval street pattern.
Chapel-en-le-Frith received its market charter in 1225, one of the oldest in the Peak District.
The town's name means 'chapel in the forest', reflecting its origins within a royal hunting ground.
It sits at the southern edge of the Dark Peak moors.
Chinley was once a significant railway junction, though most of its lines have since closed.
The village sits beneath Kinder Scout, the highest point in the Peak District.
Chinley remains a popular base for walkers heading into the Dark Peak.
Marple Aqueduct carries the Peak Forest Canal high above the River Goyt.
A flight of 16 locks lifts the canal steeply through the town.
Marple sits on the edge of Greater Manchester, close to the Peak District.
Stockport's Victorian railway viaduct, completed in 1840, dominates the town's skyline with 27 brick arches.
Beneath the town, tunnels once used as air raid shelters sheltered thousands during the Manchester Blitz.
Stockport was historically a major centre of hat manufacturing.
Alderley Edge is a wooded sandstone escarpment linked to legends of a wizard and sleeping knights.
Author Alan Garner drew on local folklore here for his novel The Weirdstone of Brisingamen.
The area has a long history of copper mining dating back to the Bronze Age.
Quarry Bank Mill, near Wilmslow, is one of the best-preserved Georgian cotton mills in England.
The mill and its worker housing offer a rare insight into early industrial working life.
Wilmslow is one of the wealthiest towns in the North West, part of Cheshire's 'Golden Triangle'.
Local legend claims the town once sold its Bible fund to buy a new bear for bear-baiting, earning it the nickname 'Congleton Bear Town'.
Congleton was historically a centre of silk and cotton milling.
The town sits on the River Dane in Cheshire.
The Sandbach Crosses are two elaborately carved Anglo-Saxon stone crosses, dating from around the 9th century.
They stand in the town's cobbled market square.
Sandbach hosts one of Cheshire's oldest chartered markets.
Northwich grew around Cheshire's extensive rock salt deposits, mined since Roman times.
Subsidence from historic salt extraction shaped much of the town's unusual architecture, including moveable buildings.
The Lion Salt Works, nearby, preserves the area's open-pan salt-making heritage.
The Eccles cake, a spiced currant pastry, has been made in the town since at least the 18th century.
Eccles sits on the Manchester Ship Canal, west of the city centre.
The original Eccles cake shop is said to date back to 1793.
Barrow's shipyard has built Royal Navy submarines since the late 19th century, including the UK's nuclear deterrent fleet.
The Dock Museum tells the story of the town's rapid growth around iron and shipbuilding.
Barrow was once the largest steelworks in the world during the 1870s.
Comedian Stan Laurel, of Laurel and Hardy, was born in Ulverston in 1890.
The Laurel and Hardy Museum in the town holds one of the world's largest collections related to the duo.
Ulverston also has a distinctive lighthouse-like monument, the Hoad Monument, on a hill above the town.
Grange-over-Sands developed as a genteel Victorian resort after the railway arrived in 1857.
Its promenade overlooks the treacherous tidal sands of Morecambe Bay.
The town benefits from a notably mild microclimate, allowing subtropical plants to grow.

landmark: Pendle Hill & witch trial heritage (via Colne)
facts: Pendle Hill is associated with the 1612 Pendle witch trials, among the most famous in English history.
Colne is the birthplace of Wallace Hartley, bandleader on the Titanic.
The town sits at the northern edge of the Lancashire Pennines.
Clitheroe Castle has one of the smallest Norman keeps in England, perched on a limestone outcrop.
The town sits in the Ribble Valley, an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty.
Clitheroe is the terminus of a scenic branch line from Blackburn.
Whalley Abbey was a major Cistercian monastery until its dissolution in 1537.
The village's 48-arch railway viaduct is one of the longest in Lancashire.
Whalley sits in the Ribble Valley, close to Clitheroe.
Accrington brick, exceptionally hard-wearing, was used in the foundations of the Empire State Building.
The town's football club gave its name to the phrase 'Accrington Stanley', once used to mean an underdog.
Accrington grew rapidly during the cotton weaving boom of the 19th century.
Blackburn Cathedral combines a Victorian Gothic nave with a striking modern lantern tower added in the 1960s and 70s.
Blackburn was one of the great cotton-weaving towns of Lancashire.
The town's name is thought to derive from a stream once described as 'black burn'.

landmark: Bolton's Le Mans Crescent & Market Hall
facts: Bolton's Victorian Market Hall, opened in 1855, remains a bustling covered market today.
The town was a major cotton-spinning centre, home to inventor Samuel Crompton, creator of the spinning mule.
Bolton's Le Mans Crescent, a grand civic building, is named for its French twin town.
Bury, near Bolton, is renowned for its large open-air market and traditional black pudding.
The town is connected to Manchester by the East Lancashire heritage railway as well as modern tram links.
Bolton is the nearest mainline station serving the wider area.
Hale is one of the most affluent suburbs in Greater Manchester, part of Cheshire's commuter belt.
The village retains an attractive traditional high street.
Hale sits close to Altrincham on the Manchester to Chester line.
Altrincham's Market House was regenerated into an award-winning food hall in the 2010s.
The town received its market charter in 1290, one of the oldest in the North West.
Altrincham is a major interchange between rail and Manchester's tram network.
Poynton is part of Cheshire's affluent 'Golden Triangle' of commuter towns.
The village hosts one of the largest one-day agricultural shows in the North West.
Poynton sits close to the Peak District boundary.
Hazel Grove developed as a residential suburb on the southeastern edge of Stockport.
Torkington Park preserves woodland and parkland close to the town centre.
The area sits close to the boundary of the Peak District National Park.
The Torrs Gorge, right beside New Mills, is a dramatic wooded ravine formed by two rivers meeting.
A network of Victorian mill buildings once lined the gorge, powered by the rivers below.
New Mills sits on the western edge of the Peak District.

landmark: Whaley Bridge & the Peak Forest Canal terminus
facts: Whaley Bridge marks the terminus of the Peak Forest Canal, close to the Cromford and High Peak Railway's old route.
The town's reservoir made international headlines in 2019 after dam damage forced a major evacuation.
Whaley Bridge sits at the western edge of the Peak District.
Leyland gave its name to Leyland Motors, once one of Britain's largest truck and bus manufacturers.
The British Commercial Vehicle Museum preserves this history in the town.
Leyland sits between Preston and Chorley in Lancashire.

landmark: Chorley's flat cap and market heritage
facts: Chorley's large indoor and outdoor markets have traded for centuries.
The town is closely associated with the flat cap as a symbol of Lancashire working-class identity.
Chorley sits close to the West Pennine Moors.
The Sankey Viaduct, near Earlestown, was part of the original Liverpool and Manchester Railway of 1830.
It was one of the earliest major railway viaducts built anywhere in the world.
Earlestown grew as a railway town around wagon works established in the 19th century.
Warrington's ornate Golden Gates were originally made for an 1862 London exhibition before being installed in the town.
Warrington sits on the River Mersey, historically a key crossing point between Liverpool and Manchester.
The town has been a New Town designation area since 1968, expanding significantly since.
The Silver Jubilee Bridge links Widnes and Runcorn across the River Mersey.
Widnes was a major centre of the British chemical industry from the 19th century.
The town developed rapidly around the Leblanc process for making soda ash.

landmark: St Helens & the World of Glass
facts: St Helens has been a centre of British glassmaking since Pilkington Brothers began production in 1826.
The World of Glass museum tells the story of the town's industry.
St Helens Junction is one of two stations serving the town, on the Liverpool to Manchester line.
Levenshulme has become known for its vibrant independent market and food scene in recent years.
The area was historically a hub for print and textile trades on the edge of Manchester.
Levenshulme sits on the line between Manchester Piccadilly and Stockport.
Horwich was built around a huge Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway locomotive works, opened in 1886.
The former works site is now home to the Middlebrook retail and leisure park.
Horwich Parkway station opened in 1999 to serve the redeveloped site.
